stories.headline: Kawhi investigation fallout: How the Clippers' roster is affected
stories.summary: After being punished for cap circumvention in 2000, Minnesota went nearly two decades without any playoff success. Is the same in store for Steve Ballmer's franchise?
stories.body:
From a team-building perspective, the most ruinous element of the NBA's punishment of the LA Clippers for salary cap circumvention surrounding Kawhi Leonard is the loss of five first-round draft picks, one each in 2029, 2030, 2031, 2032 and 2033.

There is only one precedent for such a serious punishment in NBA history: when the league similarly revoked five first-round picks from the Minnesota Timberwolves in 2000 for salary cap circumvention. In that case, the Timberwolves had come to an illegal agreement with free agent big man Joe Smith. (Then-commissioner David Stern ultimately returned two of the first-round picks.)

Looking back at how Minnesota navigated -- and suffered from -- that forfeiture can help inform our understanding of how the Clippers might fare in the years to come, as they bear the brunt of the NBA's discipline.

Minnesota's precedent
For the Timberwolves, the turn of the millennium was a terrible time to suffer such a drastic punishment. They'd been the NBA's worst team for years after joining as an expansion franchise in 1989; for the first seven years of their existence, they never won more than 29 games in a season.

But in 1995, they drafted high schooler Kevin Garnett with the No. 5 pick, and their trajectory finally started to improve. The Timberwolves won 21 games in 1994-95, the season before Garnett was drafted, but steadily rose to 50 wins by 1999-00.

Then the hammer came down, and the Timberwolves lost their first-round picks from 2001 through 2005.

Their win totals soon stalled out. After winning 50 games in 1999-2000, the Timberwolves won 47, 50 and 51 games over the next three seasons -- strong records still, but no longer showing evidence of further progression.

Minnesota finally took a leap in the 2003-04 campaign, after offseason trades for Sam Cassell and Latrell Sprewell. The Timberwolves won 58 games and landed the West's No. 1 seed, and Garnett won MVP. Minnesota went on to reach the conference finals -- winning the franchise's first two playoff series in the process -- before falling to the Lakers in six games.

But that one superlative season proved to be the Timberwolves' high point as a franchise (at least until the 2020s). Minnesota dropped to 44 wins and missed the playoffs in 2004-05, then peeled off 12 consecutive losing seasons through 2017. Garnett was traded to Boston during that drought, and it took more than a decade to recover.

So, how did the Smith sanctions ultimately affect Minnesota? On the one hand, the team still reached the playoffs in each of the next four seasons after they were levied, culminating in a conference finals run.

But on the other hand, it's hard not to wonder how much more competitive the Timberwolves could have been atop the Western Conference, and how much longer their run could have lasted, had they been able to make first-round picks during those lost draft years. Losing all of those picks conceivably cost the Timberwolves a title.

Garnett was a 24-year-old just entering his prime in 2000, but Minnesota didn't have the resources to add more young talent around him. In 2003-04, it was the third-oldest team in the NBA, according to Basketball Reference. And from 2001 through 2005, only three Timberwolves age 25 or younger averaged double-digit points in a season: Garnett himself, Wally Szczerbiak (the No. 6 pick in 1999, before the Smith case) and Chauncey Billups, a free agent signing who'd leave for Detroit the following summer.

The Timberwolves ended up selecting seven players in the draft from 2001 through 2005: five second-rounders and two first-rounders. Only one of those seven players provided even modest production in Minnesota, and that was too little, too late for the Garnett era.

Why the Clippers' future could be better -- or much worse

The comparison between the Timberwolves in 2000 and the Clippers in 2026 isn't perfect, for reasons that could provide both optimism and deep pessimism for Clippers fans.

On the positive side, seeing how the Timberwolves continued reaching the playoffs, and even reached their first conference finals, despite the lack of draft picks should be encouraging. And while the Timberwolves were devoid of first-round picks for half a decade after their punishment -- until the NBA returned two of them -- the Clippers' cupboard isn't bare, especially if their trade of Leonard back to Toronto goes through, now that the NBA has completed its investigation.

They still have a first-round pick next summer. (The Thunder can swap first-round picks with the Clippers in 2027, but the Clippers can then swap with the Raptors, per the reported terms of the Leonard trade.) And even as the NBA takes away one pick from five consecutive drafts starting in 2029, the Clippers should still have picks in 2029, 2031 and 2033, due to holding extras from the Leonard and Ivica Zubac trades.

The Clippers also managed to add a prized prospect to their team just under the wire, when they selected Keaton Wagler with the No. 5 pick in June. And their future cap sheet looks squeaky clean, giving them the theoretical ability to make upgrades in free agency -- if any star player is willing to join a franchise that was so recently embroiled in scandal.

But there are also numerous disadvantages for the Clippers, even relative to what Minnesota experienced after the Smith punishment. Most notably, the Timberwolves were a 50-win team that revolved around a young future MVP at the time, and his brilliance is the main reason that Minnesota remained competitive in its years without picks.

Conversely, the Clippers are coming off a season in which they missed the playoffs, and they're in the process of trading their best player. While Darius Garland and Wagler are both full of potential, neither guard is likely to approach Garnett's individual heights.

Moreover, the Garnett-era Timberwolves' best season came after they landed Cassell -- who made the All-NBA second team in Minnesota -- and Sprewell in trades. But they didn't need to trade a single draft pick to acquire those veteran contributors.

That was a different time; now, almost every win-now trade involves draft picks headed the other way. Yet the Clippers can't make those deals for the foreseeable future. Even if they have a few picks from other teams, the Stepien rule forbids them from trading those selections.

In other words, the Clippers have no trade flexibility for the foreseeable future, even if they see potential avenues to improve their roster.

And while the Timberwolves' loss of draft picks started immediately -- the NBA's ruling came in 2000 and began with the 2001 draft -- the Clippers' won't kick in for another three years, which means it will extend even farther into the future. If there's light at the end of the tunnel, it's a long ways away.

It's possible that the NBA could mellow its harsh discipline over time and return some of the Clippers' picks. There is some precedent here, not only from the Timberwolves receiving this grace in the early 2000s, but also from the 1980s, when the NBA gave the Cleveland Cavaliers "bonus" draft selections in 1983, 1984, 1985 and 1986 after owner Ted Stepien had traded all of Cleveland's picks away.

But that's a dim silver lining, because at the moment, the Clippers' situation looks even more dire than the Timberwolves' did a quarter-century ago. Hopefully their fans enjoyed their team's trip to the conference finals in 2021 -- which Leonard infamously missed due to a knee injury -- because it could be a long, long time before the franchise is competitive enough to return.

stories.headline: What we learned: Pressure can win Hawks the flag; the massive warning sign for Freo
stories.summary: The Hawks' outstanding pressure can win them a premiership, but the Dockers have a big problem after a 'morale-sapping' home qualifying final loss. Here's three things we learned from Hawthorn's win over Fremantle.
stories.body:
Hawthorn produced a stunning performance Thursday evening at Optus Stadium to upset minor premier Fremantle and advance to a second successive preliminary final.

Sam Mitchell's side will now enjoy the week off before returning to the MCG to hunt a place in the 2026 AFL Grand Final. Meanwhile, the Dockers will face the winner of Geelong and Carlton next week in a must-win semifinal.

Here are three things we learned from the game:

Hawthorn's relentless pressure can win the flag
It was a masterclass of pressure and intensity from the Hawks on Thursday evening in the west as they put the Dockers to the sword on their home deck to book their ticket to the final four once again.

The Hawks played the wet-dry conditions perfectly and completely stymied the minor premiers for four quarters. Sam Mitchell's side brought the heat from the opening siren, pressing up and hunting in packs, while never allowing their opponents a moment to breathe and settle into the contest.

They locked the ball inside their attacking forward 50 and had Fremantle's back six under siege for most of the evening, forcing the Dockers into 32 defensive half turnovers -- their most in a game all year. Neither the Docker defense, nor the midfield group, had any answers to stop the onslaught as they again buckled under the finals spotlight.

Mabior Chol set the standard in the opening minutes with two gut-busting efforts inside forward 50. His fleet-footed brigade of small forwards never stood still for a second, while co-captain Jai Newcombe and Dylan Moore were in-and-under all night long, combining for 14 tackles.

It was this insatiable intent and appetite for the contest that allowed Hawthorn to pile on six consecutive goals following Luke Jackson's early opener. The Hawks took a 33-point advantage into the main break, restricting Fremantle to that lone Jackson major. The margin remained the same at the final change and could only be cut to 32 by the final siren.

Thursday's performance was proof the stat sheet can sometimes be a tad misleading. The Dockers dominated total disposals (+74) and enjoyed an advantage in inside 50s (+6), while the clearance and contested possession counts were virtually identical. And yet this game only ever looked like having one victor.

Hawthorn will now enjoy a well-earned week off before returning to the MCG for a preliminary final. The three most likely opponents for that game all reside outside Victoria. If the home crowd support can be paired with the ferocity displayed against Fremantle, there's no reason they can't jag two more wins in 2026.

We should be seriously worried about these Dockers
Fremantle had been the team of the season. Minor premiers with 19 wins and four losses. An even more imposing record at Optus Stadium where they were unbeaten in 12 games, including a sensational come-from-behind win against these Hawks back in Round 9.

Unfortunately for Justin Longmuir and the legion of fans decked head to toe in purple, the Dockers waited until September to turn in their biggest stinker of the year. The Hawks played this game like the final it was and the all-conquering home side never appeared close to being up for the occasion.

Aside from All-Australian running defender Jordan Clark and the reliable Andrew Brayshaw, Fremantle had few winners on the night. Midfielders Shai Bolton and Caleb Serong were well below their best, Murphy Reid left his kicking boots at home, while forward pair Josh Treacy and Jye Amiss were just about unsighted throughout.

Thursday evening was Fremantle's lowest score of the season (40), while the 17 points scored from turnover were the fewest they had managed in a game since 2019 (excluding season 2020 which featured shortened quarters). It was also the club's second-worst game of the year for converting scores from inside 50s.

Fremantle will now have to pick themselves up, dust themselves off, and regroup for a do-or-die semifinal against either Geelong or Carlton next weekend. And while they'll likely be favoured to win that game, would anyone be tipping them with a high degree of confidence?

The loss to the Hawks is as morale-sapping as it gets. Not only because it undoes so much of the great work that was done throughout the year. Not because for them to lift the premiership they'd have to win three straight games, including two on the other side of the country. But because this club, and its supporter base, was adamant it had turned the corner following last year's disappointing home elimination final defeat to Gold Coast.

That one-point loss to end last year's campaign could prove costly 12 months on. All of a sudden the Dockers have lost two finals in a row on their home deck and will be sweating at the prospect of it becoming three in a row next weekend. Meanwhile, what would the Cats or Blues really have to lose?

If you don't want James Sicily at his worst, you don't deserve him at his best
Sure, at times he can play the role of the ultimate villain, but Hawthorn co-captain James Sicily can also be the coolest head you're likely to find behind the ball and one of the greatest assets in football come September.

On Thursday evening he was very much the latter. Sicily was simply sensational against the Dockers, leading the defensive group that completely nullified Fremantle's dangerous three-pronged attack.

Time and time again Sicily out-positioned and out-bodied the Fremantle forwards, drawing on all of his experience and smarts to put on a defensive clinic. He was always in the right place at the right time, always a step ahead of his opponent, and always composed with Sherrin in hand.

Sicily finished his night in the west with a team-high 26 disposals, a game-high 12 intercept possessions, 10 marks, and seven score involvements -- more than any player wearing brown and gold not named Nick Watson.

"We wanted to commit to being tough and taking the game on," Sicily told Fox Sports after the win. "The way we were in sync tonight is just going to give us so much confidence."

There's more than a few Hawks that can make claims to being their club's most important player, but it's hard to look past Sicily when he's in this type of form.

stories.headline: Matías Galarza joins Inter Miami from River Plate
stories.summary: Matías Galarza has joined Inter Miami CF from Argentinian side River Plate.
stories.body:
Matías Galarza officially joined Inter Miami CF from Argentinian side River Plate on Thursday.

The Paraguay midfielder signed a contract with Inter Miami on Wednesday night, officially securing Galarza's move to South Florida on the final day of the MLS transfer window.

Galarza is familiar with MLS have completed a season on loan with Atlanta United FC earlier this year. He recorded one assist in 13 appearances for Atlanta across all competitions -- including MLS regular season games and U.S. Open Cup play.

Galarza also played an integral role for Paraguay at the 2026 FIFA World Cup, scoring one goal in a group stage match against Türkiye and an assist in a shocking round of 32 win over Germany.

Galarza becomes Inter Miami's second signing on deadline day, joining Brazilian winger Riquelme Fillipi, whose deal was confirmed earlier on Wednesday.

The two players join the club as new head coach Cristian Gonzalez takes over for interim manager Guillermo Hoyos.

Inter Miami made several roster moves during this window, with a source confirming to ESPN that defender Noah Allen is set to join the Chicago Fire FC. The two clubs are in advanced negotiations, with a deal set to be finalized shortly.

The MLS secondary transfer window closed at midnight on Wednesday.

Allen was absent from Inter Miami training on Wednesday morning.

Inter Miami also loaned midfielder David Ruiz to the New York Red Bulls, with the Herons receiving $75,000 in 2027 general allocation money for the deal. The Red Bulls also hold the option to make Ruiz's move permanent at the end of the current season.

Inter Miami sits in second place on the Eastern Conference table with 42 points in 22 games.

stories.headline: Why Lewis Hamilton brought his dream Ferrari F40 road car and his iconic arrival at Italian GP
stories.summary: Lewis Hamilton shares the story behind buying his dream Ferrari F40 road car.
stories.body:
"Original paint, 69 kilometres on the clock, passenger door never opened." It's the dream listing for anyone in the market for a Ferrari F40 and all three details were among those that convinced Lewis Hamilton to open his chequebook and buy his dream car.

The seven-time champion revealed last year that he had sold off the vast majority of his car collection, saying at the time he was "more into art." But he still hankered after a pristine F40 -- a car that he, along with millions of other car enthusiasts around the world, considers art in its own right.

Roughly 1,315 F40s were built between 1987 and 1992, making low-mileage examples rare in 2026. Two weeks ago, a U.S. market model (distinguishable by black plastic trim on its front bumper) sold at auction for $8.4M with just 320 miles on the clock. Although Hamilton did not disclose the price he paid, with just 69 kilometres (43 miles) on the clock, it's possible his European market car (arguably the more desirable of the two) could have been in the same ballpark.

One feature that is coveted among collectors of all variants of F40 is the original paintwork. To save weight, the car's original paint was applied so thinly over the bodywork that the weave of the Kevlar and carbonfibre underneath is visible under the right lighting. If you can't see the weave, it's likely the paint has been reapplied at some point in the car's life and the value has dropped.

Hamilton said the red paintwork of his F40 was among a number of points on his checklist when was searching for his "dream car."

"I've been looking for one for a while and I wanted one with low mileage," he said after arriving for the Italian Grand Prix's media day in the car.

"I wanted one with a story, and lots have come up in auction over the past couple of years, some with low mileage, but just not particularly special, or maybe the paint's been redone or something like that.

"I wanted to find the most authentic one and managed to come across this one that the owner had bought, drove it from Maranello to his home, 69 kilometres, and then parked it and never started it again. The passenger door had never been opened."

Hamilton initially kept the purchase quiet. The car in question hadn't moved for over 30 years and, despite resting under a cover, was coated in a film of dust.

Without so much as running a cloth over it, Hamilton ensured the F40 was transported to Maranello's "Classiche" department -- which restores and certifies Ferraris that are over 20 years old -- to restore it to as close to original condition as possible.

The Classiche workshop is a dreamlike space stacked full of a rotating selection of client-owned cars from the brand's history. The department has its own library with original drawings of every Ferrari ever built and can restore or manufacture new parts to replace those that have worn out or been damaged.

- Lewis Hamilton takes ownership of iconic Ferrari F40 road car

- Ferrari to run Michael Schumacher tribute livery at Italian Grand Prix

Hamilton considered treating his F40 purely as a piece of art by keeping the 30-year dust intact, but ultimately said he couldn't resist the urge to get it up and running again.

"It just had this cover on it and all this dust," he explained. "Then the decision was kind of, 'What do you do? Do you keep it as an art piece, keep it all dusty, or do you have them clean it up?' So that took me a while to decide, and then I had them redo it because I wanted to drive it.

"Because I realised, actually, what's kind of crazy is, I might be wrong, but I'm pretty sure none of the Ferrari drivers in history have ever arrived in the coolest cars that they have, you know, these iconic ones, the [250] GTO or the F40. And I was like, 'It has to be done.'"

As Ferrari's expert mechanics took the car apart, they uncovered a detail that Hamilton had not seen when he first viewed the car. What they found blew his mind.

"What was also crazy is when they were taking the car apart to check it, firstly, it stood the test of time -- everything was still working," he said. "Hardly anything had to be changed.

"And when they took the engine out, they found out the engine's number 44. It's got stamped on the engine number 44 [Hamilton's race number in F1]. I couldn't believe it. I was like, 'Did you know? You've got to be lying.'

"So, it feels very much like fate. And I thought it was a real opportunity to kind of highlight the history of Ferrari in their home country, at their race, and when am I ever going to get to do that again?"

The F40 is significant in Ferrari's history as it was the last of its road cars to be commissioned and approved by founder Enzo Ferrari before his death in 1988. Original owners include F1 legends Niki Lauda, Jacky Ickx, Gerhard Burger, John Surtees and Striling Moss, while decades later Sebastian Vettel purchased a second-hand one that had originally been allocated to Luciano Pavarotti.

Hamilton's time at Maranello is already synonymous with the V8 supercar after he posed for a photo with one outside Enzo Ferrari's farmhouse on his arrival at the team at the start of 2025. He also broke the internet with a viral video earlier this year in which he drifted a Japanese-based F40 through the streets of Tokyo while Kim Kardashian screamed in the passenger seat.

Hamilton said that when he met with Ferrari's executives after the video was published, they encouraged him to create something similar in the Luce -- the brand's controversial all-new electric offering. He politely pointed out that a Luce is not an F40.

- Monza personifies the passion that enticed Leclerc to commit his future to Ferrari

- Lightning McQueen to make F1 debut at Italian GP as safety car also gets Cars makeover

- Why does the Italian GP trophy look like a pile of washing up?

"It's such a phenomenal experience to be in amongst this brand and to see how it transcends the sport and how it's touched people all over the world, the colour and the logo and these iconic cars," he said. "I showed one of the members high up, like, the F40 I drove in Japan, and they're like, 'Oh, maybe next year you can use a Luce,' and I was like, 'It's not the same as the F40,' you know.

"I think the nostalgic, iconic curves and lines that they used to build these cars back in the day, there's just nothing quite like it. Obviously, you've got the F80, which is pretty cool, or the F50, but this one, for me, I just remember as a kid I had all these cars lined up and the red car, the F40, was the one. But it was so far from my thoughts that I'd ever have a chance to acquire one of those."

On Thursday, Hamilton's arrival in the F40 at Monza was as meticulously planned as it was iconic. Despite temperatures of over 30°C, he stepped out of the non-air-conditioned car in a dark suit and brown overcoat -- every detail of which was curated by him. The images, much like the ones outside the Maranello farmhouse, will grace the pages of Ferrari history books for years to come.

"I think arriving at the race weekends, getting to race and wear red is one thing, but outside of the sport there's so much more to do within fashion," he said. "I love getting creative and coming up with concepts that most people don't, at least within my team.

"And the image that we had, we came up with for the first image we did at Ferrari that year, the first year, that was my concept, my creation. And it was the same this weekend. I had that idea: 'I want to turn up in this style, in this suit, in this way,' to pay homage to this sport, but also just get that moment because it's never going to come again."

If Hamilton's F40 wasn't the most valuable in the world when he bought it, it almost certainly is now.

stories.headline: Fenerbahce: Mason Greenwood, Matteo Guendouzi subject of UEFA investigation
stories.summary: Mason Greenwood and Matteo Guendouzi are the subject of a disciplinary investigation by UEFA, Fenerbahce have confirmed.
stories.body:
Mason Greenwood and Matteo Guendouzi are the subject of a disciplinary investigation by UEFA, Fenerbahce have confirmed.

Fenerbahce's 2-1 win away at Lyon in a Champions League qualifier ended amid ugly scenes involving Greenwood and Guendouzi who both previously played for Marseille's rivals Lyon.

Guendouzi raised his middle finger to Lyon fans during the warmup and after the game and shouted "Allez l'OM" ("Go Marseille"), also grabbing his crotch, in wild post-match scenes. He said Lyon fans insulted his family before and during the game.

A post-match scuffle included someone wearing Lyon club colours confronting Guendouzi, before several players became involved in an incident in the tunnel.

It was unclear if UEFA's disciplinary judges will sanction the players before Fenerbahce opens the Champions League main phase next Thursday, hosting Roma. Fenerbahce's second game is at Aston Villa on Oct. 14.

A Fenerbahce statement read: "Following the UEFA Champions League playoff round second leg match, UEFA has initiated disciplinary proceedings against our players Matteo Guendouzi and Mason Greenwood, as well as against our club.

"Our club will present the necessary defences before the relevant UEFA bodies in order to protect the rights and interests of our players and Fenerbahce during this process.

"The necessary information, documents and defences regarding the process will be submitted to UEFA, and developments are being closely monitored by our club. We hereby inform the public."

Fenerbahce qualified for the Champions League for the first time since 2008-09 at Lyon's expense after a 3-2 aggregate win.

Former Manchester United striker Greenwood joined the Turkish club this summer from Marseille in a €39 million ($44.5m) deal.

stories.headline: Winners and losers of Cale Makar's $163.2 million contract
stories.summary: The deal for Colorado's franchise defenseman set a new high benchmark for NHL players, with impacts around the league.
stories.body:
Cale Makar made NHL history last week, becoming the first player to earn $20 million annually in his blockbuster contract extension with the Colorado Avalanche.

His deal is worth $163.2 million over eight seasons. The 27-year-old defenseman's average annual value is $20.8 million against the salary cap. While many anticipated Makar would reset standards with his new contract, the fallout from his deal with Colorado will impact the rest of the NHL.

Some teams, players and trends will end up winners because of it. Others ... not so much.

Here are some winners and losers of the Makar contract.

Winner: Colorado Avalanche
Obviously.

GM Joe Sakic said recently that "you can't win without superstars." That's what you'd expect to hear from a guy who won Stanley Cups as a player on teams that featured Hall of Famers such as Peter Forsberg, Ray Bourque, Rob Blake and this guy Patrick Roy in goal; but also from the guy who built a roster around Makar and center Nathan MacKinnon that produced a Stanley Cup win in 2022.

There's an argument to be made that the Avalanche have the best players in the world at center and on defense and now have them both locked up through 2031. Every team in the league is trying to build a winner. No one has that kind of foundation on which to build.

Sakic was blessed with a star defenseman who wanted to go max term (eight years) from the start of negotiations. No "wait and see" contract. No trying to sync up the end of his deal with that of a family member on another NHL team (more on that in a moment). Cale Makar wanted to give Colorado nine whacks at the piñata while he's under contract.

We can tsk-tsk the Avalanche for not leveraging that commitment into a friendlier cap hit, but the reality is that both Makar and his camp fully understood the current market and the one that Makar could create as an unrestricted free agent next summer. There was no steep discount to be had here, nor should there have been the expectation of one.

There are legit concerns about aging curves and overall health for a player who logs the kind of ice time that Makar does. Teams go into contract talks all the time with that in the back of their throats. But the inherent greatness of Makar, and this window to win with him on the blue line, outweigh those worries.

His cap hit will be recontextualized, as they all eventually are. The NHL is going to have the revenue streams from new media rights deals and at least two new teams inflating the cap during Makar's contract term. As one player agent told me: "By the time this deal is over, there will be guys in the league making $30 million per season."

Loser: Bill Guerin
First off, much respect to the Minnesota GM for facing a barrage of questions during a recent local media tour -- at the Minnesota State Fair, no less! -- about the status of his contract negotiations with Quinn Hughes. We've come to expect that kind of candor from Guerin, as both an NHL executive and U.S. national team general manager, but it's still refreshing when so many of his colleagues get camera shy during high-stakes negotiations.

Guerin told WCCO's Chad Hartman that there's "no tension" with Hughes and his agent, Pat Brisson, but refused to traffic in hypotheticals. Dan Barreiro of KFAN told Guerin he "can't trade" Hughes due to how much the Wild gave the Vancouver Canucks for the defenseman; Guerin reiterated that "we don't want to lose him and our fans don't want to lose him."

Hughes has one more season left at $7.85 million before becoming an unrestricted free agent next summer, and he's eligible to sign an extension now. If he signs before Sept. 15, he can max out at an eight-year term. If he signs as a free agent next summer, the max is six years -- although the max contract he could sign (20% of a projected $113.5 million cap in 2027-28) would be higher, at $22.7 million.

It's hard to find many around the NHL who believe Hughes will sign a long-term deal with the Wild. Most expect it'll be a three-year term that walks him up to 2030 when his brother Jack Hughes of the New Jersey Devils is an unrestricted free agent. But what about the money?

As Guerin did radio hits about Hughes amid the butter sculptures and lumberjack shows at the fair, there was one common theme: That Makar's deal impacts what Hughes could make on a new contract, but not dramatically.

"Could it affect you financially? Yeah. There's the bar with Cale Makar signing that contract in Colorado, but Quinn might be after different things. He's got different things in the life that's important to him," he told Hartman.

Guerin's theory: That Hughes has already made significant money in his career, so he can afford to make different types of decisions on his next contract. His current contract, signed in 2021, is worth $47.1 million.

"It doesn't have to be that 'Makar signed for this so he's got to sign for that.' No. He can do whatever the hell he wants because he's not going broke tomorrow," Guerin told KFAN.

Of course, Makar will have made $54 million on his current deal before starting on a $163 million contract in 2027-28.

It's possible that Guerin would have to overcompensate Hughes regardless of what Makar makes, like he did to keep Kirill Kaprizov in Minnesota. Makar's deal doesn't dramatically change the math on Hughes. It also doesn't uncomplicate what's already an extremely complicated negotiation for Guerin.

Winner: Matthew Schaefer
After just one season with the New York Islanders -- in which he was the unanimous choice for NHL rookie of the year -- Schaefer might already be in blank check territory for his next contract. The defenseman, who turns 19 this week, has that rare franchise-altering alchemy of on-ice ability and off-ice charisma that's been previously exhibited by players like Alex Ovechkin. He's that special.

And soon he'll be very, very rich.

Schaefer can sign an extension next summer as he enters the last year of his rookie contract. Islanders GM Mathieu Darche now has two contractual magnets pulling up Schaefer's salary: Makar, resetting the bar for defensemen at $20.4 million AAV; and San Jose Sharks phenom Macklin Celebrini, another transformative young player who will earn $18.8 million annually over five seasons.

Loser: Columbus Blue Jackets
The current holy trinity of NHL defensemen is Makar, Hughes and Zach Werenski, the latter of whom won the Norris Trophy last season ... and then blocked a trade to the Dallas Stars after communicating that he didn't plan on signing an extension with the Blue Jackets.

Werenski, 29, has since emphasized that he wants to remain in Columbus as long as the Blue Jackets are a playoff team that's trending in the right direction.

He's eligible to sign an extension next summer, with two years remaining on a deal that carries a $9,583,334 average annual value. The ceiling for Werenski as a 2028 free agent would be an AAV of $24.6 million. Whether or not his heart's still in Columbus could be a separate issue from whether the Blue Jackets would commit that kind of money for any player -- let alone a defenseman who will be in his early 30s by then.

Winner: Montreal Canadiens
Lane Hutson finished one point behind Cale Makar in scoring among defensemen last season. In 2027-28, when he's 23 years old, Hutson will count $11.55 million less against the salary cap than Makar does.

There are mitigating circumstances for Montreal's deal with Hutson, which he signed last October in the final season of his rookie contract. The defenseman was a 10.2(c) restricted free agent, leaving him with little leverage as a player ineligible for either an offer sheet or arbitration. But Montreal used that advantage to squeeze an eight-year deal with an $8.85 million annual cap hit out of Hutson.

It was praised as a bargain at the time -- many felt he'd at least hit $10 million AAV -- but given how the ground shifted after Makar's deal for scoring defensemen, it's an absolute steal.

This is going to be for Montreal like MacKinnon's second contract was for Colorado (seven years at $6.3 million annually): an epic underpayment of an elite player that allows his team to get a ton of other business done. Keep in mind the Avalanche won the Stanley Cup in Year 6 of that deal.

Loser: Analytics truthers
Cale Makar has been a Norris Trophy finalist in six of his seven NHL seasons, winning it twice and finishing second in the voting twice as well. He has a Calder Trophy and a Conn Smythe to his credit. He's considered the best defenseman of his generation, perhaps even the best player of his generation. Comparisons to Bobby Orr aren't met with a scoff but with respectful contemplation.

But there's another assessment of Makar -- in the present and for the duration of his contract -- that's worth considering: The one from analytics-driven skeptics who see Makar's deified status as more than a little bit owed to the greatness of MacKinnon.

Corey Sznajder had a nuanced look at this theory on All Three Zones, which included these numbers from Natural Stat Trick:

"Over the past three seasons, Makar has shared the ice with MacKinnon for 2,572 minutes compared to 1,434 minutes without him (all 5v5 by the way). In those minutes, the Avs own 58.1% of the shot attempts, 57.4% of the expected goals and 61.3% of the goals. In the minutes with Makar without MacKinnon the ice, Colorado owns only 47.3% of the shots, 48% of the expected goals and 52.2% of the goals. MacKinnon without Makar on the ice is at 56.6%, 55.7% and 66.8% in all three of those stats respectively," Sznajder wrote.

Those kinds of stats don't necessarily paint their on-ice partnership as symbiotic, but rather MacKinnon being the one driving the bus, while Makar stands over his shoulder like Keanu with Sandra Bullock in "Speed."

Obviously, the Avalanche don't care about any of this after giving Makar a record-breaking contract. He and MacKinnon are going to share the ice for Colorado until 2031 at a minimum. But this conjecture will continue to simmer in awards debates, player comparisons on social media and now in evaluating Makar under this megadeal.

Winner: player empowerment
As I wrote in June, the age of player empowerment is at hand for the NHL. We saw it in Brady Tkachuk leveraging a trade to his brother's team in South Florida, or in Dylan Larkin trying to force his way out of a long-term commitment to the Detroit Red Wings. But we also saw it in some of the mega-contracts that we signed in the offseason, with Makar's deal as the current apex.

Young stars like Celebrini ($18.8 million AAV) and Chicago's Connor Bedard ($15 million AAV) scored big in re-signing with their teams. Leo Carlsson shocked the NHL by signing a five-year, $18 million AAV offer sheet with the Philadelphia Flyers that the Anaheim Ducks matched.

(My favorite theory of the offseason, offered up by one NHL player agent: That Flyers ownership greenlit the Carlsson offer sheet as the ultimate long-term vengeance in the Cutter Gauthier drama with Anaheim. "They probably want to say, 'Hey, Philly's a good spot to be in. Don't [mess] with us.'")

There are always going to be players who take a "team-friendly" deal because the circumstances warrant it, like Connor McDavid earning less annually than Leon Draisaitl. But the ones breaking the bank are no longer the outliers, and they're going to keep breaking it. Some NHL teams are projecting the salary cap could rise to $150-$160 million by the 2031-32 season. Makar is just the beginning.

(Although, technically, Makar did just sign a team-friendly deal: $400,000 annually under the max, and one year before unrestricted free agency could have upped his ask to over $22 million annually.)

Loser: Short-term deals
Perhaps the most shocking aspect of Makar's extension wasn't the money but the term.

One hallmark of the NHL's player empowerment trend has been contract duration. Auston Matthews was one of the first huge names to go short-term, signing a five-year deal with the Toronto Maple Leafs in 2019 and then a four-year extension in 2023. Since then, Celebrini, Bedard, Carlsson and Nico Hischier of the New Jersey Devils have all signed five-year extensions, while defenseman Evan Bouchard went four years with the Edmonton Oilers.

But Makar's focus from the start of talks with the Avalanche was an eight-year term, an option that will not exist when the new CBA kicks in later this month.

"I think it gives us a lot of clarity in the sense of the direction we want to go in, hopefully being able to succeed in the next nine years, and have that stability in knowing that the contract is there and we have the pieces that we can build around," he said, via NHL.com.

Again, not everyone in the NHL can look around their locker room and see Nathan MacKinnon, with the proof of concept of having already won a Stanley Cup with him. Makar didn't have to take the "wait and see" deal that others in his tax bracket have with teams striving to become contenders. Makar knows what he has around him. And now, the Avalanche know they have Makar for the next decade.

stories.headline: Broncos fall to 45-year low despite defeating Bulldogs
stories.summary: Canterbury have rolled over with a whimper in their final NRL regular-season game as the Bulldogs fell to Brisbane in a 34-20 defeat.
stories.body:
Brisbane have brought the curtain down on their miserable NRL premiership defence with a 34-20 victory over Canterbury.

Eleven months on from their drought-breaking title, the Broncos returned to Accor Stadium on Thursday and sent Payne Haas out as a winner in his final Brisbane game before he joins South Sydney.

Haas, one of the heroes of last year's premiership, scored the opening try and was sent to the sin bin in an eventful first half that ended 10-10.

But after halftime Brisbane, who have been out of finals contention for weeks, pulled away and piled on 24 second-half points.

The victory was just Brisbane's eighth for the season, in what represents the worst return of any defending premiers since Canterbury in 1981.

The Broncos are just the third side in the NRL era to miss the finals in the year after a premiership.

Winger Josiah Karapani was a standout for the Broncos on Thursday, scoring two tries, chalking up 142m and 13 tackle busts as Canterbury's season ended with a whimper.

A large contingent of Bulldogs fans in the official crowd of 13,802 headed for the exit on the hour mark, and it would be hard to blame them after a year when it felt Canterbury took a step backwards by missing out on the top eight.

As has been the case for much of this season, the Bulldogs' attack was pedestrian and laboured, and even with 38 play-the-balls in Brisbane's 20m zone they struggled to threaten in possession.

Halfback Lachlan Galvin was one of those try-scorers - hitting back after Haas and Karapani gave Brisbane an early lead - but his suitability to wear the No. 7 alongside Stephen Crichton at five-eighth is sure to be a dominant storyline over the off-season.

Crichton had a hand in Canterbury's second through left winger Enari Tuala to level the scores going into halftime, but Brisbane kicked on from there.

Billy Walters, Ben Hunt, Jordan Riki and Karapani all touched down in the 20 minutes after halftime to give Brisbane their third win since a round-eight defeat of the Bulldogs in April.

Viliame Kikau and Galvin scored two late tries to reduce the deficit, but the fulltime scoreline flattered Canterbury, who finish the year with an 11-13 record.

stories.headline: Mark Sanchez plans to plead guilty in Indianapolis assault case
stories.summary: Former NFL quarterback and Fox broadcaster Mark Sanchez has agreed to plead guilty in connection to the alleged attack of a truck driver in Indianapolis last year.
stories.body:
Former Fox Sports analyst Mark Sanchez plans to plead guilty rather than go forward with a trial next week stemming from an October 2025 fight with a truck driver outside an Indianapolis hotel, according to court records filed Thursday.

The motion asks Marion County Superior Court to schedule a hearing for Sanchez to plead guilty and be sentenced. Online records did not indicate which charges he plans to plead guilty to.

"This is a positive development. We are finalizing an agreement with the prosecutor's office that provides a path toward resolving the state's case. We're also encouraged by the constructive conversations taking place regarding the related civil matter. There is real momentum toward bringing this entire chapter to a close," Nick Sanchez Jr., Mark Sanchez's brother and legal adviser, said in a statement.

Sanchez faces a felony battery charge, along with three misdemeanor charges, for what prosecutors have said was a fight over parking.

The ex-NFL quarterback's jury trial was scheduled to start Tuesday. The trial had been rescheduled five times since it was initially set to begin in December. Sanchez and Fox Sports also face a civil lawsuit filed by the truck driver, Perry Tole.

"We are pleased with the constructive and professional conversations we've had with Mr. Sanchez's team," attorney Matt Golitko, who represents Tole, said in a statement. "Our discussions have been productive and we're on a positive path toward an agreement that will allow the parties to move forward. Mr. Tole appreciates the progress we have achieved and looks forward to an amicable resolution."

A police affidavit alleges that Sanchez, smelling of alcohol, accosted Tole, who had backed his truck into a hotel's loading docks in downtown Indianapolis. Tole claims in his lawsuit that Sanchez entered the truck without permission, then physically blocked and shoved Tole, who then doused Sanchez with pepper spray.

When Sanchez advanced after being sprayed, Tole pulled a knife to defend himself, authorities said. Sanchez was hospitalized with stab wounds to his upper right torso while Tole suffered a face laceration, according to a police affidavit.

Sanchez told police at the hospital that all he could remember was grabbing for a window, the court document said. Sanchez said he didn't know who else was involved or where the altercation happened.

Sanchez was let go by Fox Sports in November and replaced by Drew Brees. Sanchez had joined Fox Sports as a game analyst in 2021 after appearing on ABC and ESPN for two years.

Sanchez had a 10-year NFL career before retiring in 2019. He spent four seasons with the New York Jets and also appeared in games with Philadelphia, Dallas and Washington.

stories.headline: Transfer rumors, news: Liverpool to sign Camara in January?
stories.summary: After Chelsea missed out on Lamine Camara during the summer transfer window, Liverpool could try to sign him in the winter. Transfer Talk has the latest.
stories.body:
Liverpool could sign AS Monaco's Lamine Camara in January, while Chelsea have made contact with former Liverpool midfielder Georginio Wijnaldum. Join us for the latest transfer news and rumors from around the globe.

Transfers home page | Men's summer grades | Women's grades

Trending rumors

- Chelsea will face competition from Liverpool if they revive their interest in Lamine Camara, says TalkSPORT. The Reds recently contacted Camara's representatives to express an interest in signing him next summer, if a move to Stamford Bridge doesn't materialize in January. The 22-year-old is viewed as a long-term replacement for Alexis Mac Allister, who was linked with Manchester City this summer.

- Chelsea have made contact with former Liverpool midfielder Georginio Wijnaldum, Footmercato has revealed. The Netherlands international has been a free agent since leaving Saudi side Al Ettifaq, meaning the Blues can sign him at any time. Wijnaldum is viewed as a backup option to Monaco's Camara, whose proposed €55 million move to Chelsea collapsed at the final hurdle on deadline day. With the transfer window not reopening until January, the 35-year-old Wijnaldum -- who is also wanted by several Saudi clubs -- could now be their best short-term midfield option.

- Arsenal are considering a January move for AFC Bournemouth forward Junior Kroupi, according to The Independent. The 20-year-old Frenchman was on the Gunners' radar throughout the summer, but Arsenal opted against pursuing a deal before the transfer window closed. Kroupi is highly regarded at the Emirates, and the club could revisit their interest when the window reopens in January as they look to add further attacking options. Atlético Madrid's Julián Álvarez is also a player of interest, and his relationship with the Spanish club may have deteriorated further by the time the window reopens.

- Newcastle United will continue their pursuit of Bayer Leverkusen striker Christian Kofane in January, says Football Insider. The 20-year-old was also wanted by Aston Villa, but neither club were able to complete a deal before the deadline. Kofane is viewed as a player with huge upside and fits Newcastle's new recruitment strategy of targeting high-potential players. The Cameroon international scored seven goals and provided six assists last season and has already netted twice this campaign.

- Richarlison has agreed personal terms to join Trabzonspor, according to Fabrizio Romano. The Tottenham Hotspur forward has reportedly agreed a salary worth three times his current earnings at the Premier League club. Trabzonspor have already seen bids of £15 million and £20 million rejected by Tottenham, but a new proposal is expected soon as the Turkish club make the Brazilian their priority target.

stories.headline: 2026 FIBA Women's World Cup: Team USA analysis, rankings, rosters
stories.summary: Sixteen nations will compete in the World Cup in Berlin starting Friday. Team USA and France are front-runners.
stories.body:
The WNBA season is paused for the next couple of weeks, but there's plenty of women's basketball being played. The 2026 FIBA World Cup begins Friday and will run through Sept. 13 in Berlin, Germany. The tournament might not be as prominent as the Olympics -- to fans, at least -- but it is one of two major international competitions, with this year's event featuring 16 teams from North America, Europe, Asia and Africa.

The United States is, per usual, stacked, though the reigning champions suffered a blow when it was announced Monday that four-time WNBA MVP A'ja Wilson and five-time All-Star Kelsey Plum are unable to participate in the tournament due to health reasons. But those losses don't alter the task at hand: bringing home a fifth consecutive World Cup gold and 12th overall.

The U.S. women's national team plays its group phase opener Friday against China. The USA faces Italy on Sunday and then Czechia on Monday. If the U.S. women win their group, they move on to the quarterfinals on Sept. 10, with the semifinals set for Sept. 12 and the championship and third-place games on Sept. 13.

There are plenty of other familiar faces in Berlin, too, with dozens of current and former WNBA players representing other countries, from Australia to Türkiye.

ESPN's World Cup guide gets you set with everything you need to know before the games tip. Not every roster has been finalized yet, but we list current WNBA players on each squad, along with their stats for this current WNBA season.

Jump to:

HUN | ITA | JPN | KOR | MLI | NGR

PUR | ESP | TUR | USA | GROUPS

1. United States
Current WNBA players:

F/C Aliyah Boston, Indiana Fever (16.9 PPG, 8.3 RPG, 1.3 BPG)

G Paige Bueckers, Dallas Wings (20.5 PPG, 5.9 APG, 4.1 RPG)

G Sonia Citron, Washington Mystics (16.8 PPG, 4.3 APG, 1.2 SPG)

G Caitlin Clark, Indiana Fever (22.5 PPG, 8.4 APG, 3.9 RPG)

F Napheesa Collier, Minnesota Lynx (18.0 PPG, 7.3 RPG, 1.4 SPG)

F/G Kahleah Copper, Phoenix Mercury (21.3 PPG, 3.6 RPG, 1.9 APG)

G Chelsea Gray, Las Vegas Aces (12.0 PPG, 6.8 APG, 1.4 SPG)

G Rhyne Howard, Atlanta Dream (18.3 PPG, 3.6 APG, 2.3 SPG)

F Kiki Iriafen, Washington Mystics (15.3 PPG, 9.4 RPG, 0.7 SPG)

F Angel Reese, Atlanta Dream (16.1 PPG, 12.4 RPG, 1.8 SPG)

F Breanna Stewart, New York Liberty (20.4 PPG, 8.1 RPG, 1.4 BPG)

G Jackie Young, Las Vegas Aces (18.9 PPG, 6.6 APG, 4.4 RPG)

Outlook: The U.S. women's national basketball team is home to one of the most dominant dynasties in all of sports, winning eight consecutive Olympic gold medals and four straight World Cups. The program has lost just one game at a major international competition since 1994 -- the semifinals of the 2006 World Championship (later renamed World Cup) against Russia, where the Americans won bronze. Team USA has since won 30 consecutive World Cup games.

That is the legacy newly minted national team director Sue Bird, senior national team coach Kara Lawson and this young U.S. squad -- a group with seven players under 27 -- bring to Berlin. Fans have long anticipated seeing the likes of Clark, Bueckers and Reese compete against international competition as part of the senior national team. They got a taste of that at the World Cup qualifying tournament, where the USA went 5-0 and won by an average margin of 42 points.

But between the grueling schedule, heighted competition and pressure of representing the USA, the World Cup will be a much greater challenge. USA Basketball's youth movement will be tested even more so with Wilson, the reigning World Cup and Olympics MVP, and Plum no longer available. But they still have a core of experienced veterans in Stewart, Gray, Collier, Young and Copper, who know what it takes to win gold. -- Alexa Philippou

2. France
Current WNBA players:

G Pauline Astier, New York Liberty (9.2 PPG, 2.5 RPG, 3.4 APG)

F Valeriane Ayayi, Phoenix Mercury (6.3 PPG, 2.7 RPG, 1.3 APG)

G Marine Johannes, New York Liberty (8.5 PPG, 2.1 RPG, 2.4 APG)

G Leila Lacan, Connecticut Sun (11.6 PPG, 1.9 RPG, 4.6 APG)

G Carla Leite, Portland Fire (15.9 PPG, 2.1 RPG, 6.3 APG)

C Dominique Malonga, Seattle Storm (17.0 PPG, 9.0 RPG, 1.5 BPG)

F Janelle Salaun, Golden State Valkyries (12.9 PPG, 3.9 RPG, 1.2 APG)

G Gabby Williams, Golden State Valkyries (14.3 PPG, 3.3 RPG, 2.2 APG)

Other notable players: C Marieme Badiane

Outlook: France, seen as the top threat to Team USA, might have its most talented roster ever with eight active WNBA players, four of whom will be headed to the playoffs. France has been building as an international power for the last several years. The French nearly toppled Team USA in the Olympic final in Paris in 2024, falling 67-66 behind former UConn star Williams' 19 points. France also took Olympic silver in 2012 and bronze in 2021.

France's only medal in the World Cup was a bronze in 1953, the first year of the event, but they are expected to have a podium finish this year. Malonga, the 2025 No. 2 WNBA draft pick who dunked in the All-Star Game in July, might look to do that in the World Cup. -- Michael Voepel

3. Spain

Current WNBA players:

G Elena Buenavida, Minnesota Lynx (developmental player)

C Raquel Carrera, New York Liberty (1.4 PPG, 1.1 RPG, 0.3 APG)

F Maria Conde, Toronto Tempo (8.9 PPG, 4.6 RPG, 2.6 APG)

C Megan DiLeo, Portland Fire (13.2 PPG, 4.2 RPG, 0.6 BPG)

C Awa Fam, Seattle Storm (10.3 PPG, 5.7 RPG, 0.9 SPG)

G Alicia Florez, Washington Mystics (3.3 PPG, 2.0 APG, 0.6 SPG)

Other notable players: G Iyana Martin, G Maite Cazorla

Outlook: Spain has had a relatively quiet output on the international stage in recent years. They medaled at the World Cup in 2010, 2014 and 2018 and took silver at the 2016 Olympics -- but then didn't even qualify for the previous World Cup in 2022 or the podium in Paris.

Coming off a silver-medal finish at last year's EuroBasket -- and more recently giving the USA its closest game of March's qualifying tournament -- Spain could be poised for a big showing in Berlin. The team is led by veteran Alba Torrens, the only player with World Cup experience, and has a naturalized star in DiLeo, who was a top-five scorer at the 2024 Olympics. Carrera has seen limited time with the Liberty but has been much more productive with her national team. What might be most anticipated, though, is the emergence of Spain's young tandem of 20-year-old stars in Storm rookie Fam and Martin, the Fire's draft-and-stash first-round selection. -- Philippou

4. Belgium

Current WNBA players:

G Julie Allemand, Toronto Tempo (6.3 PPG, 3.1 RPG, 5.6 APG)

C Kyara Linskens, Phoenix Mercury (3.0 PPG, 2.4 RPG, 0.7 BPG)

F Antonia Delaere, Minnesota Lynx (2.9 PPG, 0.7 RPG, 1.1 APG)

Other notable players: F Emma Meesseman, G Julie Vanloo, F Bethy Mununga

Outlook: Belgium should be one of the powers of Group C, along with Australia. The Cats are coached by longtime former WNBA coach Mike Thibault, who won a title with the Washington Mystics in 2019 when Meesseman was WNBA Finals MVP. Meesseman has played nine seasons in the WNBA, most recently last year when she spent 20 games (including the playoffs) with the New York Liberty. Vanloo played briefly (five games) with the Liberty this season. This is Allemand's fourth season in the WNBA, and she has been a starter for the expansion Tempo. This is Belgium's third World Cup appearance; they finished fourth in 2018 and fifth in 2022. Belgium has not medaled at the Olympics but had its best finish in Paris in 2024, falling in the bronze medal game. -- Voepel

5. Germany

Current WNBA players:

F Frieda Buhner, Portland Fire (6.3 PPG, 2.2 RPG, 0.7 APG)

G Leonie Fiebich, New York Liberty (10.2 PPG, 3.0 RPG, 1.1 SPG)

C Luisa Geiselsoder, Portland Fire (4.5 PPG, 2.6 RPG, 1.3 APG)

F Nyara Sabally, Toronto Tempo (12.3 PPG, 5.3 RPG, 0.9 BPG)

Other notable players: F Emily Bessoir, F Lina Sontag, C Marie Gülich and G Alexis Peterson

Outlook: Just like in the Olympics, a World Cup host faces a mixture of pressure and opportunity, and it's no different for Germany in what is just its second time participating in the event (and first since 1998). Unfortunately the Germans will be without the services of star Satou Sabally, who has stepped away from basketball while recovering from the effects of her second concussion in eight months, and it's unclear how healthy her sister, Nyara, will be. For the Germans to earn their first podium finish at a major international competition, they will need a huge tournament from Fiebich, who has been showcasing her value with the Liberty upon returning from injury. But also expect the likes of Buhner and Geiselsoder to play even bigger roles than they do stateside in Portland. Germany is coached by Olaf Lange, current Tempo associate head coach and Sandy Brondello's husband. -- Philippou

6. China

Current WNBA players:

C Han Xu, New York Liberty (6.4 PPG, 2.6 RPG, 0.7 BPG)

Outlook: China should be the toughest challenger to Team USA in Group D, and the two play in the event opener for both. But the team was dealt a blow Wednesday when 6-foot-7 Dallas Wings center Li Yueru said on social media she will not be competing in Berlin because her passport was lost in the mail.

The United States and China faced off twice at the 2022 World Cup, with the U.S. women winning by 14 in group play and by 22 in the gold medal match. That result was still a win for the Chinese, though, as it marked the first time since 1994 that they earned a medal at a major international competition (both were silvers).

China faltered at the 2024 Olympics, finishing in ninth, before punching its ticket to the World Cup at this spring's qualifying tournament in Wuhan. This roster has some new faces compared to that '22 squad, headlined by the 7-foot-2, 19-year-old Zhang Ziyu. But she's not the only player who could pose some trouble for the USA, as the more experienced Han Xu (6-11) brings additional height. -- Philippou

7. Australia

Current WNBA players:

F Chloe Bibby, Minnesota Lynx (2.3 PPG, 0.7 RPG, 0.7 BPG)

G Isobel Borlase, Atlanta Dream (4.6 PPG, 1.5 RPG, 1.0 APG)

C Ezi Magbegor, Seattle Storm (6.9 PPG, 4.0 RPG, 1.2 BPG)

G Jade Melbourne, Seattle Storm (9.5 PPG, 2.2 RPG, 3.9 APG)

F Alanna Smith, Dallas Wings (6.0 PPG, 3.9 RPG, 1.0 APG)

G Miela Sowah, Golden State Valkyries (0.3 PPG, 0.8 RPG)

F Stephanie Talbot, Las Vegas Aces (3.5 PPG, 2.6 RPG, 1.0 APG)

Other notable players: F Alex Fowler, G Alex Wilson

Outlook: Phoenix Mercury guard Sami Whitcomb, captain of the Australian team, had to withdraw from the World Cup last week because of an ongoing knee injury. It's a big blow to the Opals regarding leadership and scoring. And it's heartbreaking for Whitcomb, who is 38. She was replaced by Sowah, 26. Sandy Brondello, who won WNBA titles with the Mercury (2014) and New York Liberty (2024) and is now with the Toronto Tempo, is Australia's coach.

The Opals began to emerge as an international power in women's basketball in the 1980s and won their first World Cup medal with a bronze in 1998. Their highlight was 2006, when they defeated Russia for the gold medal after the Russians had upset the United States in the semifinals. They also won bronze in 2002, 2014 and 2022, and took silver in 2018. Australia's six total World Cup medals puts them third on the all-time medal chart. The Aussies also have six Olympic medals: three silvers and three bronzes. -- Voepel

8. Italy

Current WNBA players:

G Costanza Verona, Dallas Wings (developmental player)

F Cecilia Zandalasini, Golden State Valkyries (8.8 PPG, 2.2 RPG, 1.8 APG)

Other notable players: F Lorela Cubaj

Outlook: Italy is enjoying a resurgence on the FIBA stage: Last year the team won its first EuroBasket medal since 1995 by beating France for the bronze medal, and now this World Cup marks the country's first appearance at a major international competition since the 1996 Olympics. Led by Zandalasini, the Italians lost 93-59 to the United States at the qualifying tournament in Puerto Rico, but went 4-1 overall at the event, including upsetting Spain the day after playing the U.S. women (and it's largely the same squad Italy has in Berlin). Italy has a difficult path ahead, though, having to face both the USA and China, the 2022 World Cup silver medalist, in the group phase. -- Philippou

9. Nigeria

Current WNBA players:

G/F Elizabeth Balogun, New York Liberty (developmental player)

F Amy Okonkwo, Portland Fire (4.3 PPG, 1.0 RPG, 0.3 APG)

Other notable players: F Murjanatu Musa, C Victoria Macaulay, G Ezinne Kalu

Outlook: This is the fourth time Nigeria has qualified for the World Cup, although it withdrew in 2022. That was much to the chagrin of the Nigerian players and FIBA. It was a decision by the Nigerian government, which opted in May 2022 to withdraw all its basketball teams from international competition while it restructured the sport's governance. Nigeria earned its World Cup berth this time by winning the AfroBasket 2025 championship. The team still played in the World Cup qualifying tournament in France in March, but lost three of five games. Nigeria's best finish in the World Cup is eighth, in 2018. The team's best Olympic finish is also eighth, in 2024. -- Voepel

10. Japan

Current WNBA players:

G Mai Yamamoto, Las Vegas Aces (5.8 PPG, 1.8 APG, 0.8 SPG)

Other notable players: G Rui Machida, G Kokoro Tanaka, C Ramu Tokashiki

Outlook: American basketball fans have come to enjoy Japan's entertaining style of play in recent years, particularly since squaring off against the USA in the 2020 Olympic gold medal game. Japan is known for speed, movement and 3-point shooting, which means the team can beat anyone if it gets hot -- and can lose to anyone if it can't hit shots. Lack of size is often an Achilles' heel -- just one player, Tokashiki, is listed over 6-foot.

Still, look out for the likes of Yamamoto, a midseason addition to the Aces, as well as Golden State draft pick Tanaka to make a splash on the perimeter. After the high of clinching silver at the Tokyo Olympics, Japan finished ninth at the 2022 World Cup, 12th at the Paris Olympics and almost didn't qualify for Berlin. Corey Gaines, the coach of the 2009 Phoenix Mercury championship squad, took over as head coach in early 2025. The pressure is on for them to find their form going into 2030, when they will host the next World Cup. -- Philippou

11. Hungary

Current WNBA players:

F Dorka Juhász, Minnesota Lynx (3.8 PPG, 2.6 RPG, 1.2 APG)

Other notable players: G Yvonne Turner

Outlook: While France is a big favorite in Group B, Hungary might make some waves behind Juhász. That especially could be the case with JiSu Park out for Korea and Nigeria looking kind of inconsistent entering the tournament. Hungary is making its sixth appearance in the World Cup but first since 1998. The team's best finish was fifth in 1957. -- Voepel

12. Korea

Current WNBA players:

G Jihyun Park, Los Angeles Sparks (2.2 PPG, 1.0 RPG, 0.5 APG)

Outlook: Korea is typically known as a strong outside shooting team. The team will need to rely even more on its guards with center JiSu Park, who played three seasons with the Las Vegas Aces, out due to an ankle injury. Korea is making its 18th World Cup appearance; it has played in every tournament except the first two in 1953 and 1957. Korea has won two silver medals, in 1967 and 1979. The team also has finished fourth three times, most recently in 2002. Korea has one medal in Olympic play, a silver in 1984. -- Voepel

13. Türkiye

Current WNBA players:

G/F Kennedy Burke, Connecticut Sun (8.8 PPG, 3.2 RPG, 1.4 APG)

Other notable players: G Sevgi Uzun

Outlook: Türkiye will learn a lot about its chances from its opener vs. Belgium. This is Türkiye's third appearance in the World Cup; the team was fourth in 2014, when it hosted the event, and 10th in 2018. In her seventh year in the WNBA, Burke is having a career-best season. -- Voepel

14. Mali

Current WNBA players:

F Sika Kone, Atlanta Dream (1.7 PPG, 1.0 RPG)

Outlook: Mali will make its third World Cup appearance, where it hopes to improve on an 11th-place finish in 2022. The program established itself as the second-best team out of Africa behind Nigeria, which beat Mali in the 2025 AfroBasket final. But Mali followed that up with a promising showing during the qualifying tournament in March, beating Czechia and narrowly losing to Brazil to clinch a spot in Berlin. Maimouna Haidara was the team's leading scorer in Wuhan, followed by the Dream's Kone; they'll need those two to dazzle to cause some upsets in Group A. -- Philippou

15. Czechia

Current WNBA players:

G Eliska Joklova, Minnesota Lynx (1.7 PPG, 1.1 APG, 1.0 RPG)

Outlook: Czechia is back at the World Cup after last appearing in the event in 2014; in 2010, it was the host nation and earned silver. The team's return this year has already been met with some concern. Czechia eked into the World Cup after a tepid qualifying tournament and has had some bad injury luck to two key players: Emma Cechova tore her ACL three games into her season with the Minnesota Lynx after a promising start, while Julia Reisingerova is also unavailable due to injury. On top of that, Czechia has to face the United States, China and a surging Italy squad in group play. It'll need sensational outings from the likes of Lynx rookie Joklova (née Hamzova), Veronika Vorackova and Petra Holesinska to keep up. -- Philippou

16. Puerto Rico

Current WNBA players: None

Other notable players: G Arella Guirantes, C Imani McGee-Stafford

Outlook: Host Puerto Rico was fourth in the qualifying tournament won by the United States in March in San Juan. A tough group awaits in Berlin, especially having to face Australia and Belgium. This is Puerto Rico's third appearance in the World Cup, having finished 16th in 2018 and eighth in 2022. Guirantes played two seasons in the WNBA, most recently in 2023. McGee-Stafford played four seasons in the league, most recently in 2019. Puerto Rico has competed twice in the Olympics. -- Voepel

Groups

Sixteen teams will compete in the FIBA World Cup in Berlin, Germany, with 36 games being played over 10 days from Sept. 4 to Sept. 13. The first-place team in each group advances to the quarterfinals; the second- and third-place teams will qualify for a single-game elimination format to determine the rest of the quarterfinalists.

stories.headline: Blue Jays beat Guardians 6-3 to close within a half-game of the final AL wild-card spot
stories.summary: — Brett Bateman had three hits, Nathan Lukes lined a two-run double with the bases loaded in the fifth inning and the Toronto Blue Jays moved within striking distance of the third AL wild-card spot with a 6-3 victory over the Cleveland Guardians on...
stories.body:
CLEVELAND -- — Brett Bateman had three hits, Nathan Lukes lined a two-run double with the bases loaded in the fifth inning and the Toronto Blue Jays moved within striking distance of the third AL wild-card spot with a 6-3 victory over the Cleveland Guardians on Thursday.


Toronto (70-71) has won five of six and is a half-game behind Cleveland (70-70) after taking two of three in the series. The Blue Jays also won four of six in the season series.


Tanner Bibee took a major league-leading 15th loss for the Guardians. Austin Hedges had a two-run, bases-loaded single in the fifth inning to get Cleveland within 5-3.


Angel Genao came up as the potential tying run with runners on first and second and two outs in the ninth, but Louis Varland struck him out to pick up his 32nd save in 33 opportunities. Spencer Miles (6-2) got the win.


The game was tied at 1 before Toronto sent 10 to the plate in its four-run fifth.


Ernie Clement and Brandon Valenzuela drew walks before Bateman got aboard with a bunt single down the third-base line to load the bases. Bibee (5-15) decided to make a play on the bunt, even though it appeared as if it was going to roll foul. Lukes then followed with the go-ahead hit.


Bibee, who gave up five runs on four hits, tied a career high with five walks in four-plus innings.


Toronto starter José Soriano allowed three runs on six hits in 4 2/3 innings.


Up next
Blue Jays: Head to Kansas City for a weekend series. RHP Jameson Taillon (2-6, 5.68 ERA) will start on Friday.


Guardians: Have a split doubleheader against Detroit on Friday to start a four-game set. Game 1's starter has not been determined. LHP Foster Griffin (15-4, 3.21 ERA) is expected to go in the nightcap.

stories.headline: 2026 NBA free agency: Grades for offseason signings, extensions
stories.summary: We're grading the biggest free agent signings and extensions, including DeMar DeRozan signing with the Nuggets.
stories.body:
The NBA offseason is here, and teams across the league have been busy making moves. Free agency officially began June 30.

I'm grading every free agent signing and the most impactful extensions this offseason, breaking down the ramifications for all teams and players involved.

To determine each grade, I'm looking at multiple factors, including the player's on-court impact and age, the contract's financial implications and the context of the team's short- and long-term outlooks. How risky or certain is the move? And how much does it help or hurt the team's chance to win a championship, next season or beyond?

Let's get into the latest moves:

Quick links:

Trade grades | Latest buzz | Trade machine

Depth charts | Trade tracker | More coverage

Sept 3: Rockets, Amen Thompson agree to five-year deal

Amen Thompson terms: Five years, $208 million

Grade: A-

Thompson is the second member of the 2023 draft class to sign a rookie extension this summer, following in the steps of No. 1 pick Victor Wembanyama. That order tracks, as Thompson is the second-best player from that draft class after Wembanyama.

He might not have exploded into superstardom as some expected -- and as Wembanyama did -- last season, but Thompson still fits the profile of a future two-way star. He's only 23 years old, he's one of the NBA's fiercest perimeter defenders and he boosted both his points (18.3 per game) and assists (5.3 per game) last season while leading the NBA in minutes played.

Thompson's 3-point shot remains a glaring hole in his game, as he's at just 22% from distance in his career on low volume. That weakness could limit his ultimate upside, as he might be best suited as an ace defender and offensive role player, rather than a No. 1 scoring option.

But given his present ability and future potential, extending him was a no-brainer for Houston. And as they have with other recent first-round picks, including Jabari Smith Jr., Alperen Sengun and the since-traded Jalen Green, the Rockets actually negotiated with Thompson to save some money, rather than simply presenting him with a max deal to sign.

Compare Thompson's new deal to Wembanyama's max contract, which is worth an estimated $252 million. The difference between the two extensions comes out to about $44 million over five years, or $8 million to $9 million per year -- which the Rockets can instead use to add an extra role player or help squeeze in other expensive players under the various tax thresholds.

Locking in that number for Thompson now also means the Rockets won't run the risk of paying even more for his new deal if he makes an All-NBA team (or wins Defensive Player of the Year or MVP) this upcoming season, which would have allowed him to qualify for rookie supermax status.

This deal thus carries tremendous benefits for both parties. Thompson gains generational wealth before he reaches his mid-20s, and the Rockets both retain their most talented young player for the long term and maintain a bit of financial flexibility in the process. That sounds like a win-win.

Aug. 26: Kuminga, Timberwolves agree on two-year deal
Jonathan Kuminga terms: Two years, $12.4 million, player option in Year 2

Grade: A-

Few players in recent memory have received more fanfare, relative to their on-court impact, than Kuminga. The former No. 7 pick was a key member of the Warriors' theoretical "two timelines" dynastic extension, and he was a main character of the 2025 offseason, as he lingered in restricted free agency.

A year later, however, Kuminga's new contract actually deserves the attention -- but more for the context of his new situation than because of his own development.

One of the main reasons that I was critical of the Timberwolves' trade for LaMelo Ball is that the series of transactions they used to acquire the All-Star point guard left them with a giant, gaping hole at power forward. They were already a top-heavy team without much depth, and then they parted with Julius Randle and Naz Reid in the process.

And with the LeBron James dream dashed last month, the Timberwolves had few remaining resources to acquire another frontcourt contributor. The Ball trade left them with almost no draft capital -- they have zero tradeable first-round picks, and their only tradeable second is a top-50-protected selection from Memphis in 2030 -- and they're hard-capped at the second apron, with only about $4 million in wiggle room below that barrier. (Thus, they will have to figure out a way to dump some salary before officially signing Kuminga.)

So given all those limitations, and the slim pickings nearly two months into free agency, Kuminga was clearly the best option available. The expectation is that he'll join Ball, Anthony Edwards, Jaden McDaniels and Rudy Gobert in a talented starting lineup, where Kuminga's ability to run the floor should get him enough easy buckets every game to keep his scoring average in double figures.

Kuminga isn't a perfect fit in his new role. His outside shooting struggles (33% on 3s in his career) could strain his partnership with Gobert on offense, and it's still an open question whether Kuminga will ever bring the consistency required of a nailed-down NBA starter. He has always shown flashes, but never for more than a few games or weeks at a time.

Yet on the other hand, Kuminga is still just 24 years old, and he clearly has potential if he can find the right situation in which to thrive; most recently, he was one of Atlanta's best players in the playoffs. According to ESPN's Shams Charania, other teams were interested in signing Kuminga to a larger contract this summer, which points to his continued desirability despite his flaws.

He doesn't need to be a star in Minnesota, either, but rather a competent role player. He may not even close games for his new team, whose five best players are probably Gobert, McDaniels and a trio of guards. But what the Timberwolves needed most of all was a capable power forward who can protect McDaniels -- one of the league's best perimeter defenders -- from sliding up to that position full time.

They found one, at a reasonable price. As long as Kuminga stays healthy -- he has appeared in only 83 combined games over the past two seasons -- and engaged, he'll provide a meaningful upgrade to a fringe title contender next season.

Aug. 26: Pels, Mathurin reach two-year deal

Bennedict Mathurin terms: Two years, $16 million, player option in second year

Grade: B+

The Pelicans are finally getting involved in the summer transaction cycle, after essentially sitting on their hands for the first two months of the offseason.

They picked their first spot well. Mathurin is still just 24 years old, with the potential befitting a former No. 6 pick. He's a strong individual scorer who averaged a career-high 17.6 PPG last year, and his driving ability and free throw generation remain standout skills.

Among all active non-centers with at least 5,000 career minutes, Mathurin ranks sixth in career free throw attempt rate (or the number of free throw attempts per field goal attempt). The rest of the top 10 is filled with superstars:

That said, Mathurin has been a one-dimensional player throughout his career, which holds him back from reaching the same overall level as those superstars. He has averaged only 1.9 assists per game, and he's a weak defender despite his 6-foot-5 frame.

It's notable that both the Pacers -- who saw Mathurin up close for four years -- and Clippers, who had him for half a season after the Ivica Zubac trade, were comfortable letting him go despite his youth and potential, and that Mathurin didn't attract other suitors as a restricted free agent.

But for this price and contract length, Mathurin's addition is a low-risk gamble for New Orleans, which is in need of more talent. (Expect further transactions before the season begins to create more space to fit Mathurin below the first apron.)

The second-year player option reduces some of the upside for the Pelicans, as they could lose Mathurin as early as next summer if he takes a leap under their purview. But they'd surely be thrilled if he made that leap in the first place.

Aug. 21: Thompson to join Heat after Mavs buyout
Klay Thompson terms: Two years, $13 million, player option in second year

Grade: B-

Thompson's on-court value no longer matches his name value, as a future Hall of Famer who was a centerpiece of the NBA's last great dynasty.

There's a reason, after all, that the Mavericks were amenable to buying Thompson out of the last year of his contract to pave his path to Miami. He is now 36 years old and nowhere near the sort of two-way star he was at his peak. Instead, the five-time All-Star is now a well below-average player.

DARKO Career DPM Progression

But Thompson will bring one important skill to Miami that the Heat are currently lacking: Even as he has declined, he has remained an elite shooter. Thompson has made at least 38% of his 3-pointers on high volume in every season of his career, and even coming off the bench last season, he ranked among the top 20 players in made 3s per game.

Incidentally, Thompson ranked second in total 3s from a reserve last season -- one spot behind Tim Hardaway Jr., his new teammate on Miami's perimeter.

Because the Heat already added Hardaway in free agency, it's possible that Thompson's presence will be redundant. And a two-year, $13 million deal with a second-year player option is less of an obvious win for Miami than a veteran minimum would have been.

But in truth, the Heat need all the shooting they can get around Giannis Antetokounmpo, after they lost Norman Powell and Tyler Herro, their top two shooters last season. And if any team can cover for Thompson on the defensive end, where he's now a liability because of his age and injury history, it might be a group with Antetokounmpo, Bam Adebayo, Davion Mitchell and Andrew Wiggins, to say nothing of Erik Spoelstra pulling the strategic strings.

It's still unlikely that Thompson, at this stage of his career, will be a major difference-maker for his new team. But Thompson is a better use of a roster spot than other options Miami had to complete its 2026-27 rotation.

Aug. 21: DeRozan joins Nuggets on one-year deal
DeMar DeRozan terms: One year, $3.9 million

Grade: B

Presumably, DeRozan signed this contract knowing he'd likely be asked to come off the bench in Denver, even though he has started every NBA game he has played since his rookie year -- 1,250 and counting, between the regular season and playoffs.

That shift couldn't come at a better time for the Nuggets, whose bench was incredibly depleted following the Peyton Watson sign-and-trade earlier this week. This is far from a like-for-like replacement, to be clear: DeRozan is about as different from Watson as two similarly sized players can be.
